extracted.intended_audience: IGCSE English Language students preparing Cambridge/Edexcel narrative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and marking-aligned techniques for writing short narratives in IGCSE English Language exams (Cambridge 0500 / Edexcel equivalents), including structure, language techniques, openings/endings, and exam-focused practice guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an engaging plot with a clear structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an engaging plot with a clear structure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a situation and develop it with a sense of progression so something changes (a character, situation, or reader understanding). Use an effective overall structure (see Classic Five-Part Structure or alternatives) and manage pacing so the plot feels purposeful and focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop believable characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop believable characters
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the main character at least one distinctive trait, habit, or emotion so they feel real. Use actions, body language and small details (showing) rather than exposition. Avoid flat characters by including specific character detail and motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use descriptive and literary techniques effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Use descriptive and literary techniques effectively
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a range of techniques (sensory detail, figurative language, symbolism, foreshadowing, varied sentence structure, dialogue) to deepen description and theme. Make deliberate, effective choices rather than trying to use the most complex vocabulary or every device possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with accuracy and fluency (Style and Accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style and Accuracy (up to 12 marks): Varied and effective vocabulary; Varied sentence structures used for effect; Accurate spelling, punctuation, and grammar; A consistent and appropriate register/voice
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for precise vocabulary and varied sentence forms while minimising errors. Maintain a register appropriate to the story and audience. Proofread (save ~5 minutes) for spelling, punctuation, incomplete sentences and tense consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage the reader throughout
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage the reader throughout
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hook the examiner from the opening and sustain engagement with well-chosen details, pacing, and emotional or narrative stakes. Use openings and techniques that immediately draw attention and maintain momentum towards a satisfying climax and ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classic Five-Part Structure (Exposition, Rising Action, Climax, Falling Action, Resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classic Five-Part Structure: 1. Exposition (Opening) — introduce setting, characters, situation and hook the reader; 2. Rising Action — build tension through events/complications; 3. Climax — turning point/peak tension; 4. Falling Action — aftermath and resolution of tension; 5. Resolution (Ending) — conclude (can be ambiguous or thought‑provoking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these parts to pace your story. Ensure the largest portion is rising action leading to a clear climax and meaningful resolution. Ambiguous or thought‑provoking endings are acceptable; ensure some sense of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative narrative structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative Structures: in medias res; circular narrative; flashback structure; stream of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't have to follow the five-part model. Choose an alternative when it suits your story: in medias res to start in action, circular to show change, flashback to reveal cause, stream of consciousness for focused interiority. Whichever you choose, keep a clear progression and ensure the reader understands the narrative arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, Don't Tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Show, Don't Tell
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer actions, body language and sensory detail over explicit statements of emotion. Example: replace 'Sarah was nervous' with physical/sensory detail (trembling pen, blurred words, bouncing knee). Showing puts the reader inside the experience and is more engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory Details (use all five senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensory Details — engage sight, sound, touch, smell and taste to make scenes vivid
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete sensory images (e.g., flickering bulb; door slam; cold damp stone; tang of salt; taste of copper). Sensory detail creates presence and immersion; balance senses across the scene rather than relying only on sight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figurative Language
rubrics_metrics.description: Figurative Language (simile, metaphor, personification, pathetic fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-chosen similes, metaphors and personification to elevate description (e.g., 'the silence settled like a thick blanket'). Warning: don't overload with figures of speech; two or three well-chosen devices per paragraph are more effective than many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied Sentence Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Varied Sentence Structure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence length to control rhythm and pace: short sentences for tension and emphasis, long flowing sentences for reflection/description, and occasional one-sentence paragraphs for dramatic impact. Deliberate variation strengthens style and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue — formatting and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue reveals character, advances plot and breaks up description. Follow these rules: each new speaker gets a new line; use speech marks correctly; vary dialogue tags (said/whispered/etc.) but 'said' is fine; keep dialogue natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue to show relationships and subtext; avoid unnatural, overly formal lines. Use tags and action beats to clarify who speaks without overloading with adverbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshadowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreshadowing — plant subtle hints about what’s coming to create satisfying inevitability
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert unobtrusive details that make later events feel earned. Example: remarking on an old rope bridge before it becomes important. Avoid heavy-handed or explicit hints that ruin surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolism — objects, weather or motifs can carry deeper meaning
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recurring images (storm, locked door, journey) to support theme, but avoid making symbolism too obvious; let readers discover layers themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crafting Strong Openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Crafting Strong Openings — use action, dialogue, setting/atmosphere, question/mystery or sensory openings to hook the reader
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective opening strategies include: action opening, dialogue opening, setting with atmosphere, question/mystery, sensory opening. Avoid openings like 'Once upon a time...', clichéd wake-up lines, lengthy backstory, or overtly explanatory openings such as 'This is a story about...'. Start in the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crafting Effective Endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Crafting Effective Endings — circular, ambiguous, twist, reflective, or image endings can work well
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an ending type that suits the story: circular endings show change, ambiguous endings invite thought, twist endings must be foreshadowed, reflective endings show insight, image endings close on a resonant visual. Avoid 'it was all a dream', sudden unexplained endings, unearned happy endings, or over-explaining the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and Structure (IGCSE marking criterion — up to 13 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content and Structure (up to 13 marks): Relevant and engaging content; Effective structure with a clear sense of purpose; Well-managed paragraphs with appropriate sequencing; A clear beginning, development, and ending
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To score highly, produce engaging, well-crafted and expertly structured content. Manage paragraphing to signal shifts in time/place/speaker/focus. Focus on relevant development rather than excessive backstory or irrelevant events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Band descriptors (top/middle/lower characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Band Descriptors Simplified — Top (10–13 / 10–12): engaging, well-crafted, expertly structured; precise vocabulary, varied sentences, very few errors. Middle (5–9 / 5–9): competent with some effective moments; generally accurate with some variety. Lower (1–4 / 1–4): simple, predictable, limited development; basic vocabulary, frequent errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reach the top band demonstrate control and craft — deliberate effective choices rather than gratuitous complexity. Middle band work shows competence; lower band shows limited development and frequent mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake — Trying to tell too much story
rubrics_metrics.description: Trying to Tell Too Much Story — attempting an epic when word limit is 350–600 words
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on one event or one moment and explore it deeply with rich detail rather than covering an entire saga. Plan a contained scope before writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake — All action, no description
rubrics_metrics.description: All Action, No Description — breathless sequences of events read like plot summary rather than narrative
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow down key moments to describe feelings, senses and significance. Balance action with descriptive detail and interiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake — Flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat Characters — characters lacking distinctive traits or emotional depth
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give main characters at least one distinctive trait, habit or emotion and show this through behaviour and detail rather than telling the reader directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake — Ignoring paragraphing
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignoring Paragraphing — poor paragraphing that fails to signal shifts and confuses structure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use new paragraphs for shifts in time, place, speaker or focus. Good paragraphing supports structure marks and reader clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake — Neglecting proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglecting Proofreading — failing to check for basic errors
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save 5 minutes to proofread. Check for spelling errors (commonly confused words), missing/incorrect punctuation, incomplete sentences, and verb tense consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice guidelines and exam-time advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice Prompts Guidance — plan structure (2–3 minutes); use at least three different narrative techniques; write 400–500 words; include strong opening and satisfying ending; proofread for accuracy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use targeted practice prompts to rehearse techniques. Time short planning, aim for a clear scope (one event/moment), and practise combining techniques (sensory detail, dialogue, varied sentence structure) under time constraints.
